title: The Atom You Can't Time
question: How can something so random follow such steady rules?
hook: No one can say when a single atom will decay, yet big piles of atoms keep a steady clock.
idea: A single decay is random, but many identical atoms decay at an overall rate that a half-life describes.

beats.prompt: A lone radioactive atom has existed for a very long time. You have to guess when it will decay. What does quantum theory say?

choices.label: The time cannot be predicted, however long it has existed
It is overdue, so it will decay very soon
choices.feedback: It tempts like waiting for a late bus, but age does not help: the time cannot be predicted however long the atom has existed.

choices.label: It decays at a time fixed when the atom formed
choices.feedback: It tempts because big samples look like clockwork, but that steady rate belongs to many identical atoms, not to one.

beats.explain: Decay is a random process for single atoms, and it is impossible to predict when a particular atom will decay regardless of its age.

beats.prompt: Put these steps in the story of radiation research in order.
items: Marie Curie starts studying uranium radiation
Elster and Geitel hunt for the energy source
beats.explain: X-rays came in 1895, Becquerel's discovery in 1896, Curie's study in 1897 and the energy-source experiments in 1899.

beats.prompt: match each researcher to what they did
pairs: Blackened a wrapped plate using uranium salts
Showed the rays were a property of atoms
Realized one element can turn into another
beats.explain: Each step moved radioactivity from a puzzling glow toward a property of atoms that can change one element into another.

beats.prompt: one step in this reasoning is wrong; which?
steps: A sample holds a huge number of identical radioactive atoms.
Quantum theory says nobody can predict when a single atom will decay.
So the sample as a whole can have no predictable decay rate.
Yet its overall decay can be described by a half-life.
beats.explain: Unpredictable single decays still give a predictable overall rate for many identical atoms, which is why a half-life works.
